title: Hyundai’s New 2027 Elantra Compact Sedan Just Got a Lot More Interesting

 2027 Hyundai Elantra First Look: Hyundai’s Compact Sedan Just Got a Lot More Interesting
 The new Elantra gets standout styling, a posh interior, advanced infotainment, and a revised hybrid drivetrain for 2028. 
 Aaron Gold Writer Manufacturer Photographer MotorTrend Staff Photographer Nov 19, 2026 Save
 See All 22 Photos 22 
 Our year with a sub-$25k Kia K4 has taught us how technologically advanced inexpensive sedans can be, but the new Hyundai Elantra —carrying the 2027 model year for the gas-powered model and 2028 for the Elantra Hybrid —is about to make these affordable cars a hell of a lot more interesting. Not only does the new Elantra offer Hyundai’s latest and greatest infotainment system, but it wraps it in head-turning sheetmetal with a high-luxe interior.
 0:00 / 0:00

 The new 2027 Elantra features a take on Hyundai’s emerging Art of Steel exterior styling theme as first seen on the 2027 Tucson . A riot of flat surfaces and sharp creases, Art of Steel is meant to celebrate the look of the raw sheetmetal from which the Elantra is made. We love the front end, especially the knife-edge prow, but things get a bit heavy and fussy as you move toward the back of the car. We’d prefer a proper two-box profile over the Elantra’s long roofline, but we imagine that’d kill the aerodynamics (as well as the intended resemblance to the N Vision 74 concept ). The design redeems itself out back, however, thanks to an exaggerated lip spoiler and the diffuser-like rear bumper that’s almost a parody of a hypercar, and it hints at a cheeky sense of humor.
 See All 22 Photos 22 
 Inside, the Elantra’s cabin incorporates many of the same components as the Tucson, including the furniture-inspired rounded elements on the armrests and the dashboard. The biggest difference between the two vehicles is the center console; while the Tucson goes split-level, the Elantra uses a single-level affair with a pair of wireless chargers. The Elantra’s dashboard, meanwhile, is nearly identical to the Tucson’s. The example we got to crawl around in—no doubt a top-of-the-line model though it wasn’t marked as such—had rich-feeling upholstery, which we assume is H-Tex (Hyundai’s convincing fake leather), highlighted with dramatic ambient lighting.
 ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW Hyundai, Don’t Give in to the Dark Side
 What really drew our eyes, though, was the Elantra’s massive center screen, which runs Hyundai’s new AI-enhanced Pleos system. We’ve covered Pleos extensively in this article and talked about it in our 2027 Tucson first look, but there’s a significant difference as far as the Elantra is concerned. Like the Tucson, the Elantra divides that center screen 30/70, Tesla-style, with the speedometer and basic car information on the left third and everything else (infotainment, navigation, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto) on the right two-thirds.
 See All 22 Photos 22 
 The primary difference between the Tesla central-screen-only setup and what Hyundai does is the addition of a small, ribbon-style driver’s display located above and ahead of the steering wheel. But the entry-level Elantra won’t get it, which means you’ll have to rely on the center screen for speed, turn signals, and the like. We don’t mind central displays, but some of us have struggled with the single-screen setups used by Tesla, Ineos, and the Volvo EX30, especially those of us who rely on reading glasses. (Perhaps Hyundai thinks only young people with good vision will buy the cheapest Elantra?) Admittedly, it’s not fair to condemn this setup until we’ve had a chance to try it, but given our experiences up until now, we hope Hyundai won’t follow Tesla into this tempting ocean of cost-cutting. There be sharks, Hyundai.
 ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW Same ICE, New Hybrid
 As we alluded to in our opening paragraph, the new-shape Elantra will launch with two powertrains. The Elantra’s base engine will continue to be Hyundai’s 2.0-liter four-cylinder, still putting out 147 hp and 132 lb-ft and still tied to a continuously variable automatic. Hyundai anticipates the same 35-mpg combined EPA estimate as the current car.
 The optional hybrid (remember, that’s model year 2028) will use a greatly improved powertrain. Engine displacement remains at 1.6 liters, but the electric motor gets a horsepower boost from 43 to 60. Combined output of gas engine an electric motor is now 155 hp, up from 139; as with the 2.0, Hyundai has not released a torque figure. Hyundai says to expect quicker acceleration and an EPA combined rating of 53 mpg. That’s 3 mpg better than the current standard Elantra Hybrid but a 1-mpg drop compared to the entry-level Elantra Hybrid Blue.
 ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW See All 22 Photos 22 
 What of the present Elantra’s 1.6-liter turbo engine? Gone, it seems, and we imagine the hybrid system’s extra power is supposed to make up for its loss. Hyundai made no mention of the performance-oriented Elantra N , so we can only cross our fingers and hope that entertaining little hot-rod makes its return in the not-too-distant future.
 Design Director, Please Report to My Office
 Overall, we like what we see in the 2027 (and 2028) Hyundai Elantra: basic transportation that doesn’t look basic. While we’re eager to drive it, we know that most of the Elantra’s story has been told in its stunning new look. Meanwhile, we imagine every other automaker that competes in this segment is frantically scheduling meetings with their styling departments.
